The cross-sections were computed using the Tai formulas, with corrections to the original formulas.
The vertical-to-horizontal response ratio was used to estimate the fraction of vertically oriented dipoles (fv) in the cloud.
The measured-to-computed cross-section ratio was typically around -1.5 dB ± 1 dB in the range 0.19 ≤ 2l/λ ≤ 0.37.
For dipoles near 2l/λ = 0.5 (approximately 2 inches long), the measured-to-computed ratio was -4.0 dB.
For the random orientation distribution at 2l/λ = 0.5, the average measured-to-computed ratio was -1.8 dB.
The measured vertical response was about 1 dB lower and the measured horizontal response was 3 dB lower than the computed values for the random orientation distribution at 2l/λ = 0.5.
The horizontal-vertical dipole distribution should be used for dipoles less than 3 inches long, while longer dipoles gradually shift towards the random orientation distribution.
The computed cross-sections provide an improvement in accuracy of over 40% compared to the Van Vleck method.
This improved accuracy corresponds to a 50% reduction in the weight of chaff needed to produce a given echo, which is of great importance for operational chaff system design.
Discontinuities in the fv = 0 column of the tables are due to rounding errors and will not be important in estimating actual cross-sections.
The computation program automatically inserted -59.99 dB when the vertical response was zero.
Table II provides cross-sections for various values of the parameter A (2l/a) and the dipole orientation (vertical or horizontal).
Expressions are provided to compute the expected cloud cross-sections based on the vertical-to-horizontal response ratio and the fraction of vertical dipoles.
Measurements were made on operational chaff at this laboratory to validate the computed cross-sections.
The results indicate that neither the horizontal-vertical nor the random orientation distribution completely accounts for the actual measured cross-sections.
